L19: # Hypothermia
L20: 
L21: 【15†Image: QR Code】
L22: 
L23: Full Review: Aug 2026 By【16†Daniel F. Danzl】, MD, University of Louisville School of Medicine

L29: VIEW PROFESSIONAL VERSION
L30: 
L31: 【17†GET THE QUICK FACTS】
L32: 
L33: Hypothermia (dangerously low body temperature) is often regarded as a cold injury because it can be caused or made worse by exposure to cold surroundings.
L34: 
L35:   * 【18†Symptoms】|
L36:   * 【19†Diagnosis】|
L37:   * 【20†Treatment】|
L38:   * 【21†Essentials for Older Adults: Adapting to Cold Temperatures】|
L39:   * Being in an environment that is too cold, having certain disorders, or being unable to move increases the risk of harm caused by hypothermia.
L40: 
L41:   * The person shivers at first and has difficulty moving, and later may become confused and lose awareness.
L42: 
L43:   * Getting warm and dry can lead to recovery unless the body temperature is very low.
L44:   * If the body temperature is very low, doctors may warm the person with warmed oxygen and heated fluids given intravenously or passed into the bladder, stomach, abdominal cavity, or chest cavity through plastic tubes. Doctors also provide heat to the outside of the body.
L45: 
L46: Hypothermia is most often accidental. Hypothermia that occurs in people with heart, blood vessel, and nerve disorders is likely underrecognized.
L47: Hypothermia results when the body loses more heat than can be replaced by increasing the amount of heat generated by the body through exercise or by increasing warming from external sources, such as a fire or the sun. Wind increases heat loss, as does sitting or lying on a cold surface or being immersed in water. Sudden immersion in very cold water may cause fatal hypothermia within minutes.
L48: However, a few people, mostly infants and young children, have survived for as long as 1 hour completely submerged in ice water. The shock can slow down all of the body's systems, essentially protecting the body (see 【22†Effects of submersion in cold water】). Hypothermia may also occur after prolonged exposure in only moderately cool water.
L49: People at greatest risk are those who are lying immobile in a cold environment—such as people who have had a stroke or a seizure or who are unconscious due to intoxication, those with a low blood sugar (glucose) level, or those with an injury. Because they are not moving, these people generate less heat and also are unable to leave the cold environment. Such people are at risk of becoming hypothermic even when the surrounding temperature may be only as cold as 55 or 60° F (about 13 to 16° C).
L50: The very young and the very old are at particular risk for developing hypothermia. People in these age groups often do not compensate for cold as well as young adults and are dependent on others to anticipate their needs and keep them warm. Very old adults may become hypothermic while indoors if they remain immobile in a cold room for hours. Infants lose body heat rapidly and are particularly susceptible to hypothermia.
L51: Sometimes a disorder, such as a widespread infection or underactivity of the thyroid gland (【23†hypothyroidism】), causes or contributes to hypothermia. (See also 【24†Overview of Cold Injuries】.)
L52: ## Symptoms of Hypothermia
L53: 
L54: Initial symptoms of hypothermia include intense shivering and teeth chattering. As body temperature falls further,
L55: 
L56:   * Shivering stops.
L57: 
L58:   * Movements become slow and clumsy.
L59: 
L60:   * Reaction time is longer.
L61: 
L62:   * Thinking is blurred.
L63: 
L64:   * Judgment is impaired.
L65: 
L66: These symptoms may develop so gradually that people, including companions of the affected person, do not realize what is happening. People may fall, wander off, or simply lie down to rest.
L67: When shivering stops, people become more sluggish and slip into a coma. The heart rate and breathing rate become slower and weaker. If they are very slow, the person may seem to have no signs of life (no heartbeat or attempts to breathe) even though the heart is beating very weakly. Eventually the heart does stop.
L68: 
L69: The lower the body temperature is, the higher the risk of death. Death may occur at body temperatures below 88° F (about 31° C) but is most likely to occur below 83° F (about 28° C).
L70: ## Diagnosis of Hypothermia
L71: 
L72:   * Measurement of body temperature
L73: 
L74:   * Sometimes tests for other disorders
L75: 
L76: Hypothermia is a core body temperature less than 95° F (35° C).
L77: Health care professionals diagnose hypothermia by measuring the body temperature, typically with an esophageal temperature probe or an epitympanic temperature probe. An esophageal temperature probe is inserted into the esophagus, the thin-walled, muscular channel that connects the throat with the stomach. An epitympanic probe is inserted into the ear, next to the eardrum. These devices provide continuous temperature readings.
L78: Doctors assess how severe hypothermia is based on how alert the person is or based on their temperature:
L79: 
L80:   * Mild: Alert, conscious, and shivering (body temperature 32 to 35°C or 90 to 95°F )
L81: 
L82:   * Moderate: Responsive to verbal stimuli (body temperature 28 to 32°C or 82 to 90°F)
L83: 
L84:   * Severe: Responsive to painful stimuli or unresponsive with detectable vital signs (body temperature 24 to 28°C or 75 to 82°F)
L85:   * Very severe/profound: Unresponsive with no detectable vital signs (body temperature below 24°C or 75°F)
L86: Blood and sometimes other tests are done to see whether a disorder such as an infection or hypothyroidism caused hypothermia. Tests for illicit drugs and toxic substances may be performed. Tests for infection, which can cause hypothermia in very young or old people, may also be done. If a person has no signs of life, health care professionals may use cardiac ultrasound to determine whether the heart is still beating.
L87: ## Treatment of Hypothermia
L88: 
L89:   * Drying and warming the body from the outside, by removing wet clothing and wrapping in warm blankets
L90: 
L91:   * Warming the body from the inside, by warming the air to breathe and by using warm fluids
L92: ### Treatment outside the hospital
L93: 
L94: In the early stages of hypothermia, drying the body, changing into warm, dry clothing, being covered with warm blankets, and drinking hot beverages can bring about recovery. In people who are found unconscious, further heat loss is prevented by wrapping them in a warm, dry blanket and, if possible, gently removing wet clothing and moving them to a warm place while arrangements are made for immediate transportation to a hospital.
L95: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), particularly by bystanders outside of a hospital, is recommended only if there are no signs of life, which may be very difficult to detect. For example, it may be difficult, particularly for untrained people, to detect very faint respirations and heartbeats. Often, even if no pulse can be felt and no heartbeat can be heard, the heart may be beating.
L96: Also, a person with severe hypothermia must be handled gently, because a sudden jolt may cause an 【25†irregular heart rhythm】 (arrhythmia) that could be fatal.
L97: ### Treatment in the hospital
L98: In the hospital, doctors may warm the person with warmed oxygen given by inhalation and heated fluids given intravenously or passed into the bladder, stomach, abdominal cavity, or chest cavity through plastic tubes inserted into those areas.
L99: In addition, the blood may be warmed through the process of hemodialysis (in which the blood is pumped out of the body, through a filter with a heating attachment, and back into the body) or with a heart-lung machine (which pumps blood out of the body, heats the blood, adds oxygen, and then returns the blood to the body).
L100: Doctors may need to help the person breathe by inserting a plastic breathing tube through the mouth into the windpipe (endotracheal intubation) and using 【26†mechanical ventilation】. If the heart has stopped, 【27†CPR】 is done.
L101: Because some people with hypothermia who have arrived at the hospital with no signs of life have eventually recovered following resuscitation, doctors may continue resuscitation efforts until the person is warmed or until they are sure that there is no heartbeat or other signs of life.
L102: ## Essentials for Older Adults: Adapting to Cold Temperatures
L103: 
L104: Aging takes a toll on the body’s ability to adapt to the cold. With aging, the body becomes less efficient at shivering and at diverting blood away from the surface of the body. Also, the layer of fat just under the skin thins, so there is less insulation to prevent heat loss.
L105: Disorders (such as heart and blood vessel disorders, more common in older adults) can also make the body less efficient at shivering and diverting blood and make people less able to compensate for the stress of hypothermia. The body’s ability to produce heat is also decreased by some disorders that commonly affect older adults, such as underactivity of the thyroid gland (hypothyroidism).
L106: A person who is less able to move around because of an injury or a disorder such as a stroke or arthritis is also at a greater risk of dangerous cooling, because the decreased movement generates less heat-producing muscle activity. Alcohol and certain medications, such as antidepressants, increase the risk as well.
L107: Hypothermia is usually preventable. Older adults are advised to take the following precautions:
L108: 
L109:   * Maintain a warm environment. Older adults sometimes keep their home at a lower-than-desirable temperature as a means of saving money, but the thermostat should be set at 68° F (20° C) or higher. It is especially important that the bedroom be kept warm. Fuel assistance programs and home winterization programs may help defray costs.
L110:   * Wear several layers of clothing. Clothing made of wool or synthetic materials such as polypropylene are especially useful because these materials insulate even when they become wet. Because the body loses a large amount of heat from the head, wearing a hat is important. Fingers and toes must also be protected.
L111: 
L112:   * Eat warm foods and drink warm fluids. Food provides the body with fuel to be burned, and warm fluids provide heat and prevent dehydration.
L113:   * Avoid alcoholic beverages. Alcohol dilates blood vessels in the skin, which makes the body temporarily feel warm but actually causes greater heat loss.
L114: 
L115:   * Exercise regularly, particularly when cold. Exercise can increase the body’s production of heat.
